In the 2026/27 tax year, which runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027, adults aged 18 or over can pay up to £20,000 into ISAs.

You can split that between cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, innovative finance ISAs and a Lifetime ISA. The Lifetime ISA has its own limit of £4,000. Any unused allowance does not carry forward.

From 6 April 2027, investors under 65 will be capped at £12,000 a year for cash ISAs. The overall £20,000 allowance stays the same.

More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

I can't advise on how you should split your allowance. I can pass you to an adviser if you'd like that.

The ISA allowance for 2026/27 is £20,000. The tax year runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. You must be 18 or over to use it.

You can split the allowance between cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, innovative finance ISAs and a Lifetime ISA. The Lifetime ISA has its own limit of £4,000. Any unused allowance does not carry forward.

From 6 April 2027, investors under 65 will be capped at £12,000 a year in cash ISAs. The overall £20,000 allowance stays the same.

More detail is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/
I've logged your question with an adviser, who will contact you. You can also phone the switchboard on 0117 496 0100.

You can pay up to £4,000 a year into a Lifetime ISA. That counts towards the £20,000 overall ISA allowance. The government adds a 25% bonus, up to £1,000 a year.

You can open one if you're aged 18 to 39. Withdrawals for any reason other than the permitted ones incur a 25% government charge. The permitted reasons are:
- Buying a first home costing £450,000 or less, once the account has been open for at least 12 months.
- Withdrawing from age 60.
- Being terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.

More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

A Lifetime ISA can be opened by anyone aged 18 to 39. I can't tell you which other product might suit you, because that would be advice. I can escalate this to an adviser if you'd like.

You can read more at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

The changes take effect from 6 April 2027:

- Investors under 65 can pay a maximum of £12,000 into cash ISAs each tax year. The overall £20,000 ISA allowance is unchanged, so the remainder can go into stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs. Investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit.
- Transfers from stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs into cash ISAs will no longer be permitted.
- A charge will apply to interest paid on cash held inside a stocks and shares or innovative finance ISA.
- Money already in cash ISAs is not affected by the cap.

Source: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

I can't say how this affects your own situation. For that, I can pass you to an adviser.

The evidence says that investors under the age of 65 will have their cash ISA payments capped at £12,000 each tax year. It also says that investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit. These changes are listed under "Changes from 6 April 2027".

I can't tell you your own position beyond that. If you want advice on what to do, I can escalate your question.

Under HM Revenue & Customs' guidelines, transfers between cash ISAs should take no longer than 15 working days. Other ISA transfers should take no longer than 30 calendar days. Re-registering holdings in specie can take longer if fund managers are slow to respond.

The receiving provider starts the transfer. Use their transfer process rather than withdrawing the money, or the ISA may lose its tax status. We don't charge for transfers in or out.

More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

Yes, in effect. A surviving spouse or civil partner is entitled to an additional permitted subscription equal to the value of the deceased's ISAs. This is on top of their own allowance. It applies whether or not they inherit the investments themselves.

The ISA also stays tax-free as a continuing account of a deceased investor for up to three years while the estate is administered.

The pension annual allowance is £60,000. If the total paid into your pensions in a tax year goes over it, an annual allowance charge is normally due. The total includes employer contributions and the value of any defined benefit accrual.

- **Tapering:** For high earners, the allowance tapers down to a minimum of £10,000.
- **Carry forward:** You can carry forward unused allowance from the previous three tax years. This only applies if you were a member of a registered pension scheme in those years.
- **Money purchase annual allowance:** Once you've taken taxable income flexibly from a defined contribution pension, a £10,000 money purchase annual allowance applies to further defined contribution contributions.

More detail is in the pensions guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

I can't say how this applies to your own situation. I can pass you to an adviser if you'd like that.

It also says your own contributions receive tax relief up to 100% of your relevant UK earnings in the tax year, or £3,600 gross if your earnings are lower. Basic-rate relief is added to the pension automatically. Higher- and additional-rate taxpayers claim the extra relief through their tax return. The source is the pensions guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/pensions/

For a defined contribution pension, you can start drawing from age 55. This rises to 57 from 6 April 2028. You can use flexi-access drawdown, buy an annuity, take lump sums, or combine these. Each has different tax consequences.

Yes. If the transfer value is more than £30,000, the law requires you to take appropriate independent advice before the transfer can proceed. The advice must come from a firm with Financial Conduct Authority permission to advise on pension transfers. Fernhill Wealth holds that permission.

The Financial Conduct Authority expects advisers to start from the assumption that a transfer will not be suitable. Fernhill recommends one only where it can show the transfer is clearly in your interest.

From 6 April 2027, most unused pension funds and death benefits will be included in the value of your estate for inheritance tax. Benefits passing to a spouse or civil partner, or to a registered charity, remain exempt. Dependants' scheme pensions and death-in-service benefits are outside the new rules.

If you die before age 75, benefits are normally paid free of income tax, within the lump sum and death benefit allowance of £1,073,100. If you die at or after 75, the recipient pays income tax at their marginal rate.

Fernhill Wealth charges these fees for initial financial planning:

- **Full financial plan:** £2,400, plus VAT where it applies. It covers a review of your whole financial position, a written plan with recommendations, and a meeting to go through it.
- **One-off advice on a single topic:** £1,200, plus VAT where it applies. One example is how to use allowances before the end of the tax year.

Fernhill is paid by fees agreed in advance, not by commission. The fees are confirmed in writing in your client agreement before any work begins. You can see the full fee schedule at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/fees-and-charges/

Ongoing advice is charged at 0.75% a year of the assets under advice, collected monthly from your accounts. It covers your annual review meeting, access to your adviser throughout the year, rebalancing recommendations and the quarterly reports.

If you also have discretionary investment management, that fee applies as well. Your client agreement sets out the combined cost. More detail is on the fees and charges page: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/fees-and-charges/

The complaints process has these timeframes:
